Transcript

Welcome back. We're joined today by Peter Kuznick, professor of history and director of the Nuclear Studies Institute at the American University. Uh also noteworthy, as many people might know him from the 10-part or 12-part documentary series with Oliver Stone called The Untold History of the United States. So, thank you for coming on the program. >> My pleasure, Glenn. >> So, you've stud- you've well, spent uh decades studying nuclear weapons and uh yeah, the history of nuclear

confrontation. And uh you just led a an appeal to Pope Leo regarding convening an international summit due to the well, growing threat of nuclear war. Uh I was wondering if you could flesh out this argument. Why Why do you think this is so critical at this point? >> Well, let me give a little background on this initiative. It was actually built upon Jack Gilroy. Jack Gilroy is an activist with Pax Christi and with Veterans for Peace, a

long-time peace stalwart in the United States, and he drafted a letter to Archbishop Wester, who's the archbishop for the Santa Fe region in the United States. And Wester's the most outspoken voice in the US Catholic Church for peace and nuclear abolition. So, Jack drafted a letter that I became part of uh calling on Archbishop Wester to reach out to Pope Leo to urge him to call an emergency international summit. Minimally of Putin, Xi, and Trump, the

three main nuclear powers. Because where there's so much more risk of nuclear war now than there's really ever been before. Uh so, when I was in Italy, I met with Cardinal Semeraro, who's the in charge of the committee on sanctification. Uh, he and I were at the same alternative university program that meets every summer in the Italian Alps called Tonalestate. And so, I spoke to Archbishop Semeraro,

I mean, Cardinal Semeraro, and he promised that he would hand deliver the letter to Pope Leo. So, that point, we had gone beyond the Archbishop Wester initiative, so I drafted a new appeal directly to Pope Leo. And I thought of it as working on two levels. One, to urge, cajole, encourage the Pope to call this kind of emergency summit, but secondly, to include enough information there about why the risk had grown so dangerous

that we could also use it as an educational tool to mobilize the population pretty much around the world to say, "Get off this insane path of warfare and potential nuclear warfare." So, I start the appeal by quoting Tulsi Gabbard, uh, who occasionally had some very lucid moments. And on June 10th, 2025, Tulsi released a 2 and 1/2 minute video starting off in Hiroshima and says that what happened in Hiroshima

was peanuts compared to the weapons we have today. Uh, and then she said, uh, "We're closer to nuclear annihilation today than we've ever been before. And warmongers in capitals around the world are proceeding in that direction." Then in October, Sergey Naryshkin, the head of Russia's SVR foreign intelligence agency, said that uh where civilization today is more at its most fragile moment since

World War II. And the risk of of a new World War looms greatly. So, the fact that the two intelligence chiefs understood this. Tulsi's warning was issued 2 days before Israel and the United States began bombing uh Iran in 20 2025. She must have known that was coming. But, she's been alert to this threat for a long time. Uh and then we've got this coming from other sources as well.

We've got US military leaders talking about a war the threat of war with China. Philip Davidson uh issued that warning in 2021. General Mike Minihan in 2023 said he thinks the US and China are going to be a war by 2025. Fortunately, that didn't happen. But then Admiral Buchanan said more recently that the United States can fight and win a three-front nuclear war against Russia, China, and North Korea and still

keep enough nuclear weapons in reserve to maintain its global hegemony. Now, that builds upon this discussion that's going on in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, for example, which had written three articles discussing the fact that there are now two schools of nuclear planners. The old school who believes in deterrence theory and mutually assured destruction, but a new school of nuclear planners who believes that a nuclear war can be fought and won,

which Reagan and Gorbachev denied, which people have denied more recently. But, they say that that now with advanced sonar technology, artificial intelligence, and other advanced intelligence, the US can active actually pinpoint the location of every uh Chinese and Russian nuclear submarine, preemptively knock them out, knock out in a preemptive strike the intercontinental ballistic missiles, and shoot down uh the jet the fighter uh jets that it would be dropping dropping

to drop nuclear weapons. And the US could win this. There have been people reasoning like this for decades, since the start of the nuclear age. Uh and in 2006, Lieber and Press had an article in Foreign Affairs, the journal of the Council on Foreign Relations, in which they said that the US now has a first strike capability. And we can wipe out China and Russia in a preemptive strike.

And people in Russia thought that that was official US policy. It was published in Council on Foreign Relations publication. Washington Post reported that heads were exploding in the Kremlin, cuz they thought this was official US policy. Now, maybe it is official US policy. Uh but cuz there's so much more talk about the use of nuclear weapons. Um I mean, I can go on, but you can interrupt me if you'd like, but if not, I'll I'll keep explaining why we did this.

Um we know that there's pressure on Trump. I became a columnist for Al Jazeera. The first piece that Eva and Hughes and I wrote, we've written six pieces there for Al Jazeera. Eva uh teaches at Columbia, and she's the president of the Nuclear Age Peace Foundation. She's terrific. So, the first piece we wrote was titled Breaking the Nuclear Taboo. And we reasoned why Trump, you know, who's got this massive ego and you know, as as you know, is a

pathological narcissist, he's being told by some people, Netanyahu, Stephen Miller, Pete Hegseth, maybe Marco Rubio, Sebastian Gorka, telling him, "You can go down as the greatest president in history. You've broken every custom, every norm, every tradition, US law, international law. The only taboo you haven't broken is the nuclear taboo. And every other president's been afraid to break that for 81 years, but you can do it."

And we we know for you know, as Marjorie Taylor Greene of all people just warned, Trump is contemplating and being urged to use nuclear weapons weapons, tactical weapons in Iran, which we can get into in a few minutes. Uh So, but we also know, not only is Trump under that kind of pressure, Putin is under that kind of pressure. We've seen Russian leaders talking to Putin about the need to escalate dramatically. And when Putin met with a friend of mine

a few months ago, he said that he's under enormous pressure from the hawks in Russia to act much more aggressively in Ukraine. Then we've got the recent comment by Elbridge Colby, the policy chief at the Pentagon, who just wrote last week that the United States needs if fighting breaks out in the Pacific, the US will need to resort to nuclear weapons. Partly because with the the US has depleted its missiles, depleted its interceptors,

depleted its precise precision guided munitions, and I mean there is so much more of this kind of insane talk because the likelihood and the Pentagon has been trying a war game limited nuclear war for decades and they never can do it. It always ends up in a full-scale nuclear war. And we've known forever, but especially since the 1980s and the work done on nuclear winter that even a limited nuclear war can trigger a partial nuclear winter.

As Robock and Toon and others have studied more recently, a limited nuclear war between India and Pakistan which 100 Hiroshima-sized nuclear weapons were deployed would in would burn the cities and create partial nuclear winter in which the sun's rays would be blocked from coming to the earth. We have famine, disease, and that limited nuclear war could cause up to 2 billion deaths.

But we don't have 100 nuclear weapons. We've got more than 12,000 nuclear weapons and they're not Hiroshima-sized. Most are between 7 and 70 times the size of the bomb that devastated Hiroshima. So this is a reality that as a species you know, we need to really think of this along with global warming as a planetary existential threat. What we see is Trump wanting to make America great again. Putin wanting to make Russia great

again. Xi wanting to make China great again. Modi wanting to make India great again. Netanyahu wanting to make Israel We see nationalists Who speaks for the planet? Was the question that we were posing. And we said that sometimes Lula speaks for the planet and Lula has called for in this phone conversation with Trump couple days ago, 3 days ago exactly, he called for a special emergency session of the United Nations to get us off this path of war. He's

previously called for that in meetings with Putin and Xi Jinping. So that's along the same lines of what we're calling for. We said that that sometimes Guterres, but it's mostly been Pope Leo the 14th who has raised this clarion call for humanity. And he's talking about the need to end wars, the need to for nuclear abolition, the need for a different course for mankind. So he's got a unique kind of moral authority right now. And so we're urging him through these

appeal to speak out for humanity and call on the at least the leaders of the three major nations, but there should be more also, for an emergency summit meeting to get us off this path of war and nuclear war. And the reason why I think it is realistic in this moment, the United States is bogged down in Iran. You know, the Iranians have their foot on Trump's neck and they're not letting him up and Trump has been desperately trying to either through economic

pressure or military pressure to get out of this war as quickly as he can because the US has already been defeated by Iran. But similar situation, not quite the same, but in some ways parallel with Russia in Ukraine. Where Russia's making some slow progress on the battlefield, but Ukraine has been hitting Russian oil refineries, Russian shipping, grain shipping, you know, and so

what we're seeing right now is that warfare as a means of settling disputes problems crises is increasingly irrelevant. The US, the most powerful country in the history of the world has not really won a significant war since World War II. And even that's questionable because Germany's leading the rearmament of Europe and Japan is leading the rearmament of the Pacific. So, what did we win in World War II? Uh but as since then, the US was defeated in Vietnam, in

Iraq, in Afghanistan, Libya's quagmire, Syria Where has the US had a military victory? Maybe Gulf War I, but didn't have a diplomatic victory, and maybe Operation Urgent Fury in Grenada in 1983. But and and if the US can't win in Iran and Russia has been bogged down there for 5 years in uh in Ukraine, maybe we need to find different ways to settle these disputes. And so, this is what we're asking the

Pope to do. And we're we've been getting heads of state, former heads of state, former leaders of militaries have former diplomats from around the world signing on because I think there's a universal recognition that we're on a very dangerous path and the pressure on Putin is enormous and and Trump could in his moment of desperation actually resort to using nuclear weapons cuz nothing else is working in the war in Iran. So, that's why I'm so worried. That's

why I started this initiative of building on Jack Gilroy's brilliant stroke and why we're getting such a positive response cuz people recognize this around the world, I think. >> This is This is all very similar to Dr. Strangelove it feels sometimes this kind of recklessness and yeah how how careless they are about yeah the prospect of nuclear annihilation and you know even if um well even if it can't be

achieved this nuclear first strike if leaders political and military leaders believe it can be I mean they will be much more reckless they'll be willing to go up that escalation ladder assuming that their opponent would have to fold and uh but uh let's say such a nuclear first strike would be possible knocking out all of you know Russia's thousands of nuclear weapons the Chinese the North Korean I mean we this planet is not that big we all reside here you would uh you know you would destroy it for for you know the winner as well it would be a

horrible disaster but it's just it shocks me a bit how how things we would never think about doing in the past is now commonplace almost that is uh remember those uh attacks on Russia's early nuclear warning systems then the attacks on Russia's nuclear deterrent and uh apparently the the the invasion of Russian Kursk had objective of seizing control over the Russia's Kursk nuclear power plant to use it as some kind of a leverage and as you said now there's uh well allegedly some talks in Washington about

doing a tactical nuclear strike on the Iranians hoping they will fold and again East Asia is a whole other story of its own so I guess what I wanted to ask is why is there no more fear of nuclear war I listen to our governments our media I mean that it's as if it's a minor thing something that belongs to the past it's even considered sometimes immoral to be worried about nuclear war because before we call it nuclear deterrence or the nuclear peace now we call it nuclear blackmail that is you know, in reference to Russia, if we

if we worry about nuclear war, then we're essentially empowering Putin. So, we have to strip him of this by calling his bluff. This is kind of the logic. I'm just Yeah, I'm wondering what future generations will say about the time we live in now. The you know, the war enthusiasm and the demonization. >> Somebody coming down to the earth. Remember the movie The Day the Earth Stood Still, I mean, 1951? And they got a visitor from some other galaxy, and he brings comes to bring the message of peace to Washington, and immediately lands in Washington, D.C., and the US Army shoots him.

Uh but then he has these magic healing powers, and he ends up with this threat saying that we don't care what you do on your own planet, but if you threaten the universe, we're going to turn your planet into a burned-out cinder. Yeah, but it you mentioned Dr. Strangelove. When my friend Oliver Stone was in Moscow some years ago, when he had spent 20 hours meeting with Putin for his documentaries about Putin, he asked Putin if he had seen Dr. Strangelove, and Putin said he had never had, and

Oliver showed it to him on his computer. They watched Dr. Strangelove together. But all these world leaders, you know, I often say I have For example, when Obama went to uh Hiroshima, uh from the day Obama got elected, I was urging him to go. Finally, the end of his administration in 2016, he visited. NHK, Japan's public television, brought me over there to do commentary during the Obama visit. And Obama says, uh you know, he says, uh death fell from the

skies. You know, death didn't fall from the skies. The United States dropped an atomic bomb. Then he goes on to repeat the leading myth about the atomic bombings in World War II. He says World War II reaches brutal end in Hiroshima and Nagasaki. That's the lie that's at the heart of the American empire. This idea that not only were the atomic bombs necessary because the fanatic Japanese would never have surrendered, but that they were humane cuz it saved half a million American lives and

millions of Japanese lives. That's the lie, right? Because as we know that the Japanese were desperate to surrender at that point and the US knew it. US knew that we could change the surrender terms, let them keep the emperor which they were begging for and which their cables we had intercepted were all saying uh or we could wait for the Soviet invasion. US intelligence has been saying since April that the Soviet invasion would finally convince all Japanese that

further resistance was futile. Trump Truman understood that. Truman had lunch with Stalin in Potsdam on July 17th. And he goes home and he writes in his journal, "Stalin will be in the war by August 15th. Finny Japs when that occurs." He writes home to his wife Bess the next day, "The Russians are coming in. We'll end the war a year sooner now. Think of all the kids who won't be killed." But he wanted to use the bomb. The Soviet invasion began August 9th and he would been told that, but he got the

dates wrong. But he wanted to use the bomb to send a message to the Kremlin that if they interfered with US plans in Europe or the Pacific, this is what they're going to get and worse, much worse. Leslie Groves, the head of the Manhattan Project, said that from 2 weeks from the time I took over this project, I understood that Russia was the enemy and we ran the project on that basis. Jimmy Byrnes, who become Secretary of State and Trump's and Truman's leading advisor, says the same thing. He says, "Well, we

want to roll back the Russians in Eastern Europe." The United States had eight five-star admirals and generals in 1945. Seven of the eight are on the record saying the atomic bombs were either militarily unnecessary, morally reprehensible, or both. Admiral Leahy, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Truman's personal chief of staff, said this the bombings put us on the moral level of the barbarians of the Dark Ages. And I could go on, but you know, this kind of crazy thinking has been around for a

long time. And now it's gaining a foothold again. But the point you were making was that at the end of the Cold War, people assumed or believed that the nuclear threat was now over. In the 1980s, there was tremendous concern. You know, I was on campus, I was teaching, and that was the big issue. There were all these anti-nuclear groups and all this momentum in the US. The million-person march in Central Park. In fact,

they would just unearth photographs of Pope Leo when he was a young priest participating in a 1983 German or Italian march of a million people against the positioning of the of the missiles in Europe in 1983. Leo was involved in those protests back then. So, we've had this for a long time, but people went to sleep after the Cold War ended. But in recent years, it's

happened again. One of the things I credit for the real emergence of First of all, my friend Dan Ellsberg, when he knew he was dying, he really doubled down and used every ounce of strength to warn the world about the threat of nuclear war and nuclear winter. But the Oppenheimer movie also had a catalytic effect. You know, and I was surprised I was teaching a course at American University unrelated to nuclear issues. It was right after the movie came out and I asked my students how many seen the movie Oppenheimer

thinking three or four hands would go up. 80% of the students raised their hands. You know, so this is a generation whose burning moral issue is Gaza. You know, and and they absolutely hated the Biden and Kamala Harris and Trump support for the genocide in Gaza. This was a really galvanized them, but they also are awake to planetary climate threats and to the nuclear threat. And I'm seeing a lot of momentum again in that direction. Uh when I was just in

Nagasaki on July 25th keynoting an international peace conference sponsored co-sponsored by Asahi Shimbun, the leading newspaper in Japan, the city government in late Nagasaki and the Nagasaki peace movement, six of my students went with me to Japan to Kyoto and Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Then when I went to this conference in Italy and keynoted that, 11 of my students came to that. They don't get any credit. They pay out of their own pocket, but they care. They're really

passionate in their concern about the future. And so that's what we're trying to appeal to. You know, we're saying that our generation might have screwed up in a lot of ways. The baby boomers um but, you know, and they go back to what quote-unquote the greatest generation. One of the things that Oliver Stone and I invade against is this idea of the greatest generation being so heroic. Yes, they won World War II, but they

gave us Vietnam, they gave us the planet planetary destruction, they gave us these huge military complexes. Uh and we need a very, very different kind of thinking. And Pope Leo seems to have embraced that kind of thinking. So, we're giving him as much support as we can and as much encouragement to do the right thing for humanity. And anybody else who wants to take about leadership, like Lula's been doing, we encourage that. We want people to speak for the planet

and not for this country or that country, this war or that war. We need a very, very different approach. >> Yeah, I like that the appeal was also to the Pope because at least uh uh yeah, the church has has a possibility to take an independent position. One of the things that are being has been a great concern to me is how everyone essentially's been falling into line over the past few years. That is, there's very little dissent. Any government narratives which is pushed out uh is no longer contested. And especially

with the peace movement, this is very strange to me that even peace movements are now appeasement. It's seen with suspicion about being treasonous. Uh I um yeah, I did have a think of thought though about what you said about the well, falsifying the history about the atomic bombs being used against Japan. And I can see why that I mean, nobody wants to see themselves as monsters. We all have our national narratives. I mean, you know, history should inform, but also build up, you know, national identities. But, I think in that process, we also deprive ourselves of very important lessons that, you know, we're all

capable of evil. You know, we we also have to be restrained. Instead, it's always assumed that, you know, we have to do as much as possible to restrict only to restrain others. Um but on the topic of restraint though, we we had nuclear well, arms control agreements uh during the Cold War, we kind of learned to establish some you know, rules of the game. And uh you know, Washington-Moscow eventually developed all this mechanism for crisis communication, reducing stockpiles. What they have left is, you

know, have transparency. Uh again, agreements, rules uh all of these arms controllers agreements now from, you know, START, INF, all of them appears to be melting away. And uh yeah, that's how how how does that affect the probability though of miscalculation because there's no guardrail anymore, it seems. >> Right, and there's no strategic stability talks going on either. Trump has managed Well, we start with 2002 when Bush got the United States out of the ABM treaty. And is that then that Russia began this major research on new

delivery systems and new weapon systems after the US abrogated the ABM treaty. But then Trump has torn up every other treaty, as you say. And right now, there are no treaties between the US and Russia. The first one was the partial test ban treaty in 1963. Ted Sorensen, Kennedy's speechwriter, said nothing Kennedy ever did gave him as much satisfaction as passing concluding the first nuclear arms control treaty. And when Kennedy announced it, he said

uh he's he talked about the old Chinese proverb that a journey of a thousand miles must begin with a single step. He said, "And let's take that step." That's sort of how we're viewing this. Low effort. Journey of a thousand miles has to begin somewhere. And so, let's take that step. You know, Kennedy had a lot of wisdom. What What are the things that we point to in here that Jack did even better in his letter was talking about the Cuban Missile Crisis. Cuz during the Cuban Missile Crisis, Kennedy and Khrushchev both did

everything they could to avoid a war. And they both understood that they had lost control. Khrushchev wrote Kennedy an incredible letter right after it ended on October 30th. He wrote to Kennedy and he said, "From evil, some good must come. Our people have both felt the burning flames of thermonuclear war. We have to use that to our advantage. Let's eliminate every conflict between us that could cause another crisis." And then Kennedy was a little slow, but

he finally responded. And he gave that And he asked Norman Cousins, who had gone there twice as intermediary, to met with Khrushchev twice. And Khrushchev said, "You know, if there's a new If war breaks out, what difference will it make if we're capitalists or communists, if we're Russians or Americans or Chinese or Italians? Who'll be left to tell us apart? Who'll be there to tell us apart? You know? And so, Kennedy made that great speech at American University. I think it was

June 10th, 1963. And his peace speech, in which he calls for an end to the the nuclear arms race, calls for an end to the Cold War. And and But the thing about that speech, he didn't let the Pentagon see it. He didn't let the State Department see it. He didn't let the intelligence community see it. It was drafted by Norman Cousins and by Ted Sorensen and Kennedy himself. And it was the I think the greatest presidential speech of the 20th century. So, but no American president has spoken

with that same clarity of vision, that same moral impetus that Kennedy had the last year of his life. Yeah, and sometimes Obama said good things, but we've seen very little of that kind of vision. But the American people have to demand it. And we need that kind of grassroots movement again. But since the So, what the point I wanted to make before I got sidetracked was that during the Cuban Missile Crisis, Pope John the 23rd issued a private

appeal to Kennedy and Khrushchev. Uh he used his moral authority to say, "Let's end this peacefully. Let's not start World War III." And Khrushchev actually cited the appeal from the Pope. And he said that gave him some of the cover that he needed to back down on the Cuban Missile Crisis. Sadly, Soviet leaders drew a different lesson that they never wanted to be have to back down and from a position of weakness. And they built up their

nuclear arsenal in order to match the United States. And then we had you know, by 19 by what year? 1986, the world had 70,000 nuclear weapons. I I took students on a study abroad class in Kyoto, Hiroshima, and Nagasaki for 25 years. And the American students traveled with Japanese students through Ritsumeikan University and Meiji Gakuin University, and we studied World War II together. The US atrocities, the Japanese

atrocities against fellow Asian countries. Do you know that a big part of the of those killed in Hiroshima and Nagasaki were Korean slave laborers who the Japanese brought over who who were out there working in the fields and in the cities and were and got no support from the Japanese government and no medical care afterwards. There were close to 50,000 Korean slave laborers in Hiroshima alone the day of the atomic bombing.

Uh but this message that the Pope issued in 19 62 that we saw Pope Paul the VI issue, that Popes have made repeated statements about, have really been and the Catholic Church has been in the forefront of this effort since uh 1962. And and that's why this is something Pope Leo could do. He's shown great judgment. Aside from being a Chicago White Sox fan in American baseball, he's shown a lot of really good judgment on

different things. Uh but uh and and I think could respond and and maybe Trump and Putin are looking for a peaceful way out of these wars right now because the military solutions are really not working uh at at this point. And then you've got these crazy people like Elbridge Colby going around threatening China with nuclear war. The US just sent another uh ship through the Strait of Taiwan.

You know, but the behavior is so erratic. So Trump threatens allies. Trade war now with Canada. Threatening to bomb the has out of Oman. Kadi canceling next month's war games with South Korea. I think that's fine, but it's the crazy way that Trump does things that make everybody think that you know this build-up as you see in Europe, this re-militarization of Europe. And the statements from European leaders

Macron, Starmer, Merritt, Burnham, you know, over and over again. Uh you got um Now Rocky, the president of Poland saying Poland neither needs Poland needs his own nuclear weapons. Zelensky saying either let us join NATO or give us nuclear weapons. Tusk you know Macron extending a nuclear umbrella over Germany and other countries. This militarization in Europe is also mad. Uh France's leading military figure, General Fabian

Mandone telling uh French generals recently that the French have got have to be willing to lose their children again in order to stop Russia. But we can see these crazy statements, this re-militarization. Where are they getting the money for this? Now they want to spend up to 5% of GDP. Trump's pressuring Taiwan to spend 10% of GDP. Take the money out of housing, health care, education, you know, food programs and putting it

in the military. Why isn't anybody out there talking about diplomacy? Why does it have to be people like us talking about the need for diplomacy? Why aren't the leaders out there other than Lula and sometimes Xi Jinping talking about development and diplomacy rather than warfare? You know, it became crazy during the Biden administration. This This bipartisan warmongering in the United States. Although now the Democrats have gotten off the war path in Iran to a large extent. Not entirely, but for the

most part. >> The criminalization of diplomacy doesn't go very well with the Yeah, this kind of nuclear escalations, but the you know, I'm a bit shocked as well by this military militarism because you you know, a lot of this was predictable and uh you would thought we would have learned from history. I say predictable because you know, it was many predicted that the whole post-Cold War order would break down. That is that hegemony would be temporary. You know, we would exhausted ourselves. Eventually rivals would

appear. And then of course conflicts would break out. Panic would set in. Uh everyone would then begin to arm themselves to the teeth willing to take greater risks, even war. I mean, making matters worse we kind of had 30 years of small wars which are far away inferior opponents. Uh in a worst case we can just pull away and leave them um in a messed up situation. China, Russia, you know, maybe the Iran's not a great power, but it's certainly quite a formidable power on the southern end of the Eurasian continent. So

uh I just I don't understand Again, I know I asked a similar question before, but whenever one talks about diplomacy, they need to, you know, uh not wait until after a great war before we start to reorganize the um or adjust to new realities. those leaders, the Kennedys, the Khrushchevs, where where are they today? >> You know, all the European leaders use the Munich analogy for why we've got to arm Ukraine to the teeth and stop Russia. Cuz if they, you know, as Reuters says, you know, if Russia gets a win in Ukraine, it's coming after the rest of Europe next. And you know, that's that's the thinking. if war spreads and turns to nuclear the chances of humanity surviving are scant if if at all. So especially in the nuclear age war is absolutely and diplomacy has got to take over. You know, and the Pope calls for that and Lula and Guterres and academics like us and a lot of people are beside me our appeal and former leaders
